analysis.one_liner: Strengthens oversight of privatized military housing and extends health benefits to service families harmed by unsafe units.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, received no committee action and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Military families live in housing built and managed by private companies under a decades-old Defense Department program. This bill would require unannounced inspections by independent inspectors, replace landlord employees in on-base housing offices with military employees, let the Pentagon cancel contracts with landlords that don't fix serious breaches, publish the landlords' contract finances, and apply state and local tenant protections to on-base housing. It would also create a health registry and VA disability presumptions for illnesses tied to unsafe privatized housing, extend VA care to affected family members, and bar Armed Services Committee members and senior defense officials from owning stakes in military housing companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families living in privatized military housing get independent inspections, tenant protections, and honest maintenance records. Veterans and family members — including children exposed in utero — who developed conditions from unsafe units would gain VA health care and disability compensation presumptions. Taxpayers and troops both gain from financial transparency into how housing allowances are spent by private landlords.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Defense Department to hire independent, certified housing inspectors and to allow state and local inspectors to inspect on-base units without advance notice to the landlord, and bars a landlord from marking maintenance complete until an independent inspector signs off in writing.

Requires the Pentagon to rescind a privatization contract if the landlord fails to cure a material breach within 90 days, and bars that landlord from new contracts or expansions; housing offices on installations must be staffed only by military employees rather than landlord employees.

Extends all federal, state, and local housing protections — including habitability standards and eviction defenses — to people living on military installations, and requires the Pentagon to publish landlords' 10-K-equivalent financial statements and annual contract financial details.

Creates a screening program and public registry for service members and family members with health conditions linked to unsafe housing, establishes a VA presumption of service connection for illnesses associated with living in privatized housing, and makes affected family members eligible for VA hospital and nursing home care (subject to appropriations).

Bars Members of Congress serving on the House or Senate Armed Services Committees, senior Defense Department executives, and generals and admirals (O-7 and above) from owning any interest in a company that owns or manages privatized military housing, with civil enforcement penalties.

analysis.who_pays: The private companies that hold military housing contracts bear the cost: unannounced inspections, public financial disclosure, possible contract termination, application of local landlord-tenant laws, and a new prohibition on ownership by defense-connected officials. Taxpayers fund the new VA care and registry, though family care is capped at whatever Congress appropriates.

drawbacks.text: The health registry, disability presumptions, and family-member VA care create new federal benefit costs, and care for family members is provided only to the extent funded in advance by appropriations — so coverage could fall short of the promise.

Applying every state and local housing law to on-base units, plus allowing the Secretary to rescind contracts for uncured breaches and bar those landlords from new work, could destabilize the privatization financing model, since the program depends on long-term private landlords who recoup investment over decades.

Critics of the presumption approach generally argue that blanket disability presumptions can compensate conditions without proof of individual causation; this bill guards against that by requiring scientifically supported, statistically significant associations before any condition is presumed service-connected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The oversight provisions — inspections, honest work orders, contract enforcement, and financial disclosure — target problems service families have reported for years and are largely procedural. The costlier parts are the new VA benefits, which are limited by appropriations for family care and structured with scientific evidence standards for presumptions. The main honest objection is that stricter enforcement against landlords could strain the privatization financing model itself; the bill's answer is that the Pentagon must maintain a contingency plan to manage units if a contract is rescinded.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with only days left in the session, the bill was referred to three committees, none of which took any action, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the Military Housing Oversight and Service Member Protection Act on December 10, 2024, on behalf of herself, Rep. Marilyn Strickland, and Rep. James Moylan.
The same day, it was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and additionally to the Veterans' Affairs and Judiciary Committees.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the bill's action history.
The bill had two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private landlords holding Defense Department housing contracts are better off: they face no new independent inspections, no public financial disclosure, no state and local tenant protections on base, and no risk of contract rescission for unfixable breaches, and no ownership ban applies to defense officials. Service members and families gained nothing from the bill's failure.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — but no hearing, vote, or recorded opposition ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the fight is unknown.

industries.note: These companies own or manage on-base housing under Defense Department contracts funded by service members' housing allowances. The bill subjects them to unannounced independent inspections, public financial disclosure, state and local landlord-tenant laws, work orders they cannot close without an inspector's sign-off, and contract rescission for uncured breaches. Their gain from the bill's failure is the public's continued exposure to unsafe units.

industries.industry: Defense-connected officeholders and officials with stakes in housing companies
industries.note: The bill bans Armed Services Committee members, senior Defense Department executives, and general and flag officers from owning interests in privatized military housing companies, with civil penalties. This concern never became law, so members and officials who hold or could acquire such stakes are unaffected.
